claims.text: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical lamellar dual-phase microstructure, exemplified by FCC + B2 phases.
Internal FCC/BCC-type phase boundaries are strong barriers to dislocation motion and can accumulate dense dislocation structures.
Dislocation pile-ups at the internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle or catastrophic failure during tensile straining.
Low-temperature annealing can induce coherent nanoscale ordered L12 precipitates in a lamellar FCC + B2 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
The annealing-induced L12 precipitates will nucleate specifically along the dual-phase lamellar interfaces.
The L12 precipitates will modify local chemistry and crystallographic structure at the lamellar interfaces.
Interfacial L12 precipitates will act as additional dislocation-nucleation sources.
The additional dislocation sources will facilitate smoother dislocation transfer across the phase interfaces.
The proposed interfacial precipitates will mitigate dislocation pile-ups and lower local stress concentrations.
Lower pile-up stress will reduce microcrack initiation and brittle failure.
Annealing will significantly increase room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
Annealing will retain or increase strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Fine L12 precipitates provide strengthening through an Orowan bowing and bypass mechanism.
The intervention is applicable under room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading.
The beneficial response depends on achieving an optimal precipitate size, distribution, and coherence without substantial coarsening or phase transformation.
Overaging or precipitate coarsening may negate the proposed strength and ductility benefits.
